doc.title: Phil Schaap interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003

chapter: Becoming an audio man and DJ
title: Rock and roll, Big Al Sears and Heywood Henry
summary: He liked rock; Big Al Sears and Ruth Sears hosted him; Heywood Henry played bass sax on I Put A Spell On You.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: Did the music, let’s say the AM rock of the time, have any impact on you at all?
Yeah. I liked it a lot. Not so much maybe AM. Remember, my guys were playing for Allen Freed and loved him.

Big Al Sears, who we haven’t mentioned since I gave short shrift to the Ellingtons, let’s not forget Big Al Sears. He was great. And to spend another second in his basement if it rains or in his backyard if it’s not, would be heaven. I would even trade you one of my rarer records for just one second of that in real time again. The food from Ruth Sears, who still lives, although like she doesn’t cook up a feast anymore, I think she’s like ninety something. But she still lives in the house. And Big Al Sears had gone into the record business and become quite an executive, and it was rock & roll. And he was wonderful to me. I’m glad to have something nice to say about rock & roll, it made me mention Big Al Sears in a jazz interview.
Well it’s great because a lot of those fellas would get work in the studios even, playing.
Yeah. Heywood Henry is on “I Put A Spell On You” and that’s the first time he ever—
Heywood Henry of the Erskine Hawkins band [scats] they had to rent a bass saxophone for him to play that. That’s a bass sax.
Being played by a great baritone saxophonist.
I’ll be darned. Well after we’re done I have to ask you about if you know who a certain saxophone player is.
Yeah I’ll let you run the show for this here. We’re running out of tape.
